name: Conversational Implicature
statement: We mean more than we say: hearers infer the rest from the assumption that we are cooperating.
statementAccent: We mean more than we say
meaning: Conversational implicature is a notion introduced by the philosopher H. P. Grice for what a speaker implies, suggests, or means by an utterance over and above what they literally say. It is part of speaker meaning that goes beyond the literal semantic content, what is said, and is worked out, or calculated, by the hearer using general principles of conversation rather than being encoded in the meanings of the words. Grice developed the idea in his William James Lectures at Harvard in 1967, especially the lecture Logic and Conversation, later collected in his 1989 book Studies in the Way of Words. At the heart of his account is the Cooperative Principle: make your conversational contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange in which you are engaged. Under this principle Grice grouped four categories of maxims, named after Kant: Quantity, be as informative as required but no more; Quality, be truthful, saying neither what you believe false nor what you lack evidence for; Relation, be relevant; and Manner, be perspicuous, avoiding obscurity and ambiguity and being brief and orderly. Implicatures arise especially when a speaker openly flouts a maxim while remaining cooperative, prompting the hearer to infer an intended meaning. Grice also distinguished conversational from conventional implicature.
mechanism: Conversational implicature works through the interaction of the Cooperative Principle and its maxims with the hearer's reasoning. Speakers are presumed to be cooperating, contributing what the purpose of the talk requires, so a hearer expects contributions to respect the maxims of Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner. When a speaker says something that, taken literally, seems to violate a maxim, yet is presumed still to be cooperating, the hearer infers that the speaker must mean something beyond the literal content, an implicature that restores the assumption of cooperation. A key mechanism is flouting: openly and conspicuously failing to fulfill a maxim in a way the hearer is meant to notice. A tutor who writes a reference letter praising only a candidate's punctuality and handwriting flouts the maxim of Quantity, saying far less than would be relevant if the candidate were strong, and thereby implicates that the candidate is weak; irony and metaphor work by flouting Quality, saying something patently false so that the hearer infers a different intended meaning. Grice distinguished such conversational implicatures, which depend on context and general principles, from conventional implicatures, which are tied to the meanings of particular words like but or therefore. Conversational implicatures have characteristic properties: they are cancelable or defeasible, since the speaker can add a clause that withdraws them without contradiction; non-detachable, since they attach to what is said rather than to the exact words; calculable, since the hearer can reconstruct the reasoning; and non-conventional, not part of the literal meaning.

examples.text: A reference letter praising only a candidate's punctuality flouts Quantity and implicates that they are otherwise weak.
Irony and metaphor say something patently false, flouting Quality, so the hearer infers a different intended meaning.
An implicature can be canceled without contradiction, as in some but not all, or some and in fact all, marking it as pragmatic.

variants.name: The maxims
variants.text: Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner, the four categories of conversational maxims under the Cooperative Principle.

variants.name: Conversational versus conventional
variants.text: Context-dependent, cancelable conversational implicature versus conventional implicature tied to words like but and therefore.

whyItMatters: Conversational implicature is one of the founding ideas of modern pragmatics and a central tool in the philosophy of language for understanding how communication outruns literal meaning. Grice was the first to study systematically the gap between what a sentence means and what a speaker means by uttering it, and his framework of the Cooperative Principle and the maxims gave a precise, general account of how hearers routinely infer far more than the words strictly encode. This clarified the crucial distinction between semantics, the literal content of what is said, and pragmatics, what is communicated in context, a distinction that organizes much of the study of meaning. The theory explains a vast range of everyday phenomena, from irony, understatement, and hints to the way we read between the lines of a tactful reply, and its diagnostic properties, especially cancelability, give a rigorous test for whether a piece of meaning is pragmatic rather than semantic. Grice's work reshaped linguistics, the philosophy of language, and cognitive science, and it underlies later theories of communication and inference. As the account of how we mean more than we say and hearers work out the rest, conversational implicature is a cornerstone of the theory of language use.

working.text: take the speaker to be observing the Cooperative Principle and its maxims of quantity, quality, relation, and manner.
observe where the literal utterance seems to violate a maxim while the speaker remains cooperative.
work out the further meaning the speaker must intend to restore the assumption of cooperation.

limits: Grice's theory, though foundational, leaves open questions and faces refinements. The exact status and completeness of the maxims are debated, and later theorists, notably in relevance theory, have tried to reduce the several maxims to a single principle of relevance, arguing that Grice's list is redundant or imprecise. The boundary between what is said and what is implicated is itself contested, since some apparently pragmatic contributions seem to intrude into literal content, a problem pursued in debates over the semantics-pragmatics interface. Determining which implicature a flout generates depends heavily on context and shared background, and the reasoning hearers actually perform is not always as tidy as the calculability requirement suggests. Some historical details reward care, such as the 1967 lectures, the 1975 publication of Logic and Conversation, and the 1989 collection, and the precise wording of the Cooperative Principle and the maxims should be quoted from Grice rather than paraphrased loosely. So conversational implicature robustly explains how speakers mean more than they say, understood as a seminal framework whose maxims and semantics-pragmatics boundary remain under active refinement.
misreadings: Conversational implicature is not part of the literal meaning of the words; it is inferred from what is said together with the assumption of cooperation, and it can be canceled without contradiction, unlike entailment. The maxims are not rules speakers must never break, since much implicature arises precisely by openly flouting a maxim. And conversational implicature differs from conventional implicature, which is tied to specific words, so treating implicature as literal content, the maxims as inviolable rules, or all implicature as conventional, misreads Grice's account.
origin: H. P. Grice's notion, from his 1967 lectures and Studies in the Way of Words (1989), of what a speaker means beyond what is literally said, worked out by hearers via the Cooperative Principle and the maxims of conversation.

sources.text: Implicature, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Grice's distinction between what is said and what is implicated, the Cooperative Principle, the maxims of Quantity, Quality, Relation, and Manner named after Kant, implicature by flouting, the conversational versus conventional distinction, and the properties of cancelability, non-detachability, and calculability.

Paul Grice, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Grice's 1967 William James Lectures, Logic and Conversation, Studies in the Way of Words (1989), and the theory of conversational implicature and speaker meaning.
